q: What is the percent atom economy of this Wittig reaction for making methylenecyclohexane? Molar masses (g/mol): cyclohexanone 98.15, Ph<sub>3</sub>P=CH<sub>2</sub> 276.32, methylenecyclohexane 96.17, Ph<sub>3</sub>P=O 278.29.
h: Atom economy = (mass of the desired product ÷ total mass of all reactants) × 100%. Which product is the one you want?
w: Atom economy = 96.17 ÷ (98.15 + 276.32) × 100% = 96.17 ÷ 374.47 × 100% = 26%. The large triphenylphosphine oxide by-product carries away about three quarters of the reactant mass. This is why the Wittig reaction scores poorly on atom economy even when its yield is high.
x: 74% is the mass fraction that ends up in Ph<sub>3</sub>P=O, the by-product. Atom economy uses the mass of the desired product, methylenecyclohexane.
98% divides the product by the ketone alone. Every reactant counts, and the ylide is by far the heaviest.
100% would require every reactant atom to end up in the product, as in an addition or Diels–Alder reaction. Here Ph<sub>3</sub>P=O is lost.

q:
Three routes to cyclohexanol are shown (catalysts not counted). Rank them from lowest to highest atom economy. Molar masses (g/mol): cyclohexanol 100.16, cyclohexene 82.15, H2O 18.02, bromocyclohexane 163.06, NaOH 40.00, cyclohexyl acetate 142.20.
I. cyclohexene + H2O (H2SO4 catalyst) → cyclohexanol
II. bromocyclohexane + NaOH → cyclohexanol + NaBr
III. cyclohexyl acetate + NaOH → cyclohexanol + CH3CO2Na
h: Divide 100.16 by the total reactant mass for each route. An addition reaction with a catalyst loses nothing.
w: I: 100.16 ÷ (82.15 + 18.02) = 100% (an addition; the catalyst is not counted). II: 100.16 ÷ (163.06 + 40.00) = 49%; the heavy Br leaves as NaBr. III: 100.16 ÷ (142.20 + 40.00) = 55%; sodium acetate is lost. II < III < I.
x: This swaps II and III. The bromide route loses the heavier by-product share (49% vs 55%), so it is the lowest.
This reverses the ranking. Substitutions and hydrolyses that release salts lose mass; the catalyzed hydration keeps every atom.
Hydration (I) is an addition with 100% atom economy, so it must be the highest, not in the middle.

q: A lab oxidizes cyclohexanol to cyclohexanone with stoichiometric Na<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> in aqueous H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>. Which change best follows the principles of green chemistry?
c: Use catalytic TEMPO with aqueous NaOCl (bleach) as the oxidant, which leaves mainly NaCl and water as by-products
Use PCC in dichloromethane instead, so the oxidation does not need water
Use twice as much Na<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> so that all the alcohol reacts faster
Run the chromic acid oxidation in benzene so that the product is easier to separate
h: Look for the option that replaces a toxic, stoichiometric reagent with a catalyst and a benign oxidant.
w: Chromium(VI) reagents are toxic, carcinogenic and used in stoichiometric amounts, leaving chromium waste. Catalytic TEMPO with bleach oxidizes secondary alcohols to ketones using a catalyst (principle 9), a less hazardous reagent (principle 3) and gives mainly NaCl and water as waste (prevent waste, principle 1).
x: PCC is still a stoichiometric Cr(VI) reagent, and dichloromethane is a chlorinated solvent; this is not greener.
More chromium means more toxic waste and lower atom economy; it works against the principles.
Benzene is a carcinogenic solvent, and the toxic chromium reagent remains; this makes the process less green.

q: Ethane-1,2-diamine and benzene-1,4-dicarbonyl dichloride (terephthaloyl chloride) are combined. What repeat unit forms in the step-growth polymer, and what small molecule is released at each link?
h: Each link is a nucleophilic acyl substitution of an amine on an acid chloride. What leaves?
w: Each NH2 attacks a COCl carbon; chloride leaves and the N–H proton is lost, so each new amide bond releases one HCl. Alternating diamine and diacid units give a polyamide: –[NH–CH2CH2–NH–CO–C6H4–CO]n–, releasing HCl.
x: Water is released when a diamine is condensed with a dicarboxylic acid at high temperature. With an acid chloride the leaving group is Cl<sup>−</sup>, so HCl is lost.
This is a polyester, which would need a diol (ethane-1,2-diol). The monomer here has NH<sub>2</sub> groups, so amide links form.
Acyl substitution keeps the C=O carbon; only Cl leaves. Nitrogen bonds to the carbonyl carbon, not directly to the ring.

q: Poly(lactic acid), a compostable plastic made from corn sugar, has the repeat unit –[O–CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)–CO]<sub>n</sub>–. Which monomer gives this polymer by step-growth condensation with loss of water?
h: Each ester link joins the OH of one monomer to the COOH of the next. Where is the CH<sub>3</sub> in the repeat unit?
w: In the repeat unit the CH bearing CH3 sits between the ester oxygen and the C=O. The monomer must have OH and COOH on adjacent carbons with a methyl on the OH carbon: 2-hydroxypropanoic acid (lactic acid). Head-to-tail esterification releases one H2O per link.
x: 3-Hydroxypropanoic acid would give –[O–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>–CO]<sub>n</sub>–, with no methyl branch.
Acrylic acid polymerizes by chain growth through its C=C and loses no water; it gives a C–C backbone with CO<sub>2</sub>H side groups, not an ester backbone.
Propane-1,2-diol has two OH groups and no carbonyl, so it cannot form ester links with itself.

q:
Which polymers are made by step-growth (condensation) polymerization?
I. polystyrene, from styrene (C6H5CH=CH2) with a radical initiator
II. a polyamide from ethane-1,2-diamine and decanedioyl dichloride, releasing HCl
III. poly(ethylene terephthalate), from dimethyl terephthalate and ethane-1,2-diol, releasing CH3OH
h: Step-growth polymers link two different functional groups and usually lose a small molecule; chain-growth polymers add monomers across C=C bonds.
w: I is false: styrene adds across its C=C in a radical chain reaction (chain growth), and nothing is lost. II is true: amine + acid chloride links form amides and release HCl. III is true: transesterification forms ester links and releases methanol. II and III only.
x: This leaves out II. Amide formation from an acid chloride is a condensation that releases HCl at every link.
This includes polystyrene, a chain-growth (addition) polymer with no by-product, and leaves out PET.
Polystyrene is not a condensation polymer; radical addition across C=C is chain growth.

q: The Fischer projection shows D-ribose. What are the CIP configurations of its stereocenters?
h: In a Fischer projection H is on a horizontal (toward you) bond. Find the 1→2→3 direction, then reverse it.
w: At each center, OH ranks first and H last. At C2 the order is OH > CHO > C3; at C3, OH > C2 (O,O,H) > C4 (O,C,H); at C4, OH > C3 > CH2OH. With all OH on the right and H on a horizontal bond, each 1→2→3 path appears counterclockwise; because H points toward the viewer, reverse it. Every center is R: 2R, 3R, 4R.
x: All-S is L-ribose, the mirror image. With H toward the viewer the apparent direction must be reversed.
This is D-xylose, which has its C3 OH on the left. In ribose all three OH groups are on the right.
This is D-arabinose, with its C2 OH on the left.

q: The Fischer projection shows D-allose. Which structure is β-D-allopyranose?
h: D-allose differs from D-glucose only at C3. In the β anomer of a D-pyranose, the anomeric OH is on the same face as the CH<sub>2</sub>OH.
w: Cyclization uses the C5 OH, so C2–C5 keep their configurations: in D-allose all four are R in the open chain, and in the pyranose C2, C3 and C5 are R while C4 is S. The β anomer has the C1 OH cis to the C5 CH2OH (C1 is R). The correct structure has C1 R, C2 R, C3 R, C4 S, C5 R: β-D-allopyranose. In a Haworth drawing, all four ring OH groups and the CH2OH point up.
x: This is the α anomer: only the anomeric carbon is inverted, so its OH is trans to the CH<sub>2</sub>OH.
This is β-D-glucopyranose. Its C3 OH is on the opposite face (C3 S); allose and glucose are C3 epimers.
Every stereocenter is inverted, so this is the enantiomer, β-L-allopyranose.

q:
Which compounds are reducing sugars (give a positive Benedict's test)?
I. maltose, α-D-Glcp-(1→4)-D-Glcp
II. methyl β-D-galactopyranoside
III. trehalose, α-D-Glcp-(1→1)-α-D-Glcp
h: A sugar is reducing only if some anomeric carbon is a hemiacetal (one ring O plus one free OH), which can open to the aldehyde.
w: I is reducing: the glycosidic bond uses C1 of the first glucose and C4 of the second, so the second unit's C1 is still a hemiacetal that opens to an aldehyde and reduces Cu2+. II is not: C1 carries OCH3, so it is an acetal (glycoside) that cannot open in base. III is not: the 1→1 link ties up both anomeric carbons as acetals. I only.
x: Trehalose is joined through both C1 atoms, so it has no hemiacetal left. Like sucrose, it is non-reducing.
This reverses I and II. The methyl glycoside is an acetal, while maltose keeps a free anomeric OH.
Glycosides (II) and 1→1-linked disaccharides (III) have no hemiacetal, so they cannot open to the aldehyde.

q: Amylose (starch) and cellulose are both unbranched polymers of D-glucopyranose joined 1→4. Why can humans digest amylose but not cellulose?
c: Amylose has α(1→4) glycosidic bonds, which human enzymes hydrolyze; cellulose has β(1→4) bonds, which they cannot
Amylose is made of D-glucose and cellulose is made of L-glucose
Cellulose links C1 to C6, which makes its chains too branched for enzymes
Amylose units are hemiacetals, while cellulose units are acetals
h: The two polymers share the same monomer and linkage positions. What is left to differ at the anomeric carbon?
w: Both polymers are made of D-glucose linked C1→C4. The difference is the anomeric configuration: α(1→4) in amylose and β(1→4) in cellulose. Human amylases hydrolyze α-glycosides only. The β links also let cellulose chains lie flat and H-bond into rigid fibers.
x: Both polymers are made of D-glucose; neither uses L-sugars.
Cellulose is linked 1→4, not 1→6, and it is unbranched. The 1→6 branches belong to amylopectin and glycogen.
In both polymers every internal link is an acetal (glycoside). Only the chain end has a hemiacetal.

q: L-Cysteine has pK<sub>a</sub> values of 1.96 (COOH), 8.18 (SH) and 10.28 (NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>). Which structure is the major form at pH 12?
h: A group is mostly deprotonated when the pH is above its pK<sub>a</sub>. Compare 12 with each pK<sub>a</sub>.
w: pH 12 is above all three pKa values, so each acidic group has lost its proton: CO2−, S− and neutral NH2. The dianion H2N–CH(CH2S−)–CO2−, net charge −2.
x: The thiol (pK<sub>a</sub> 8.18) is deprotonated at pH 12, almost four units above its pK<sub>a</sub>.
The ammonium group (pK<sub>a</sub> 10.28) is mostly deprotonated at pH 12, so the nitrogen is a neutral NH<sub>2</sub>.
This zwitterion is the major form near the isoelectric point (about pH 5), not in strong base.

q: A mixture of four amino acids is separated by electrophoresis in a buffer at pH 4.5. Which one moves toward the anode (the positive electrode)? Isoelectric points: aspartic acid 2.8, glycine 6.0, histidine 7.6, lysine 9.7.
h: An amino acid is negatively charged when the pH is above its pI, and negative ions move toward the positive electrode.
w: At a pH above its pI an amino acid carries a net negative charge; below its pI, a net positive charge. Only aspartic acid (pI 2.8) has a pI below 4.5, so only it is anionic and migrates to the anode: aspartic acid. Glycine, histidine and lysine are net positive at pH 4.5 and move toward the cathode, lysine fastest.
x: pH 4.5 is below glycine's pI (6.0), so glycine carries a small net positive charge and drifts toward the cathode.
With pI 7.6, histidine is net positive at pH 4.5 (its imidazole is protonated) and moves toward the cathode.
Lysine (pI 9.7) is the most positive of the four at pH 4.5 and moves fastest toward the cathode.

q: In an α-helix, what holds each turn of the helix in place?
c: Hydrogen bonds from each backbone C=O to the N–H of the residue four positions further along the same chain
Disulfide bonds between cysteine side chains on adjacent turns
Hydrogen bonds between backbone groups on two separate, side-by-side strands
Ionic attractions between the free N-terminal NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> and C-terminal CO<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> groups
h: Secondary structure is held by backbone–backbone interactions. In a helix, are they within one strand or between strands?
w: The α-helix is a secondary structure held together by backbone hydrogen bonds within one chain: the C=O of residue i accepts an H-bond from the N–H of residue i + 4. These bonds run almost parallel to the helix axis, about 3.6 residues per turn. Side chains point outward.
x: Disulfide bridges are covalent cross-links that help fix tertiary (or quaternary) structure. Many helices contain no cysteine.
H-bonds between neighboring strands describe a β-pleated sheet, not a helix.
There is only one N-terminus and one C-terminus per chain; they cannot hold every turn of a helix.

q: Proline residues are rarely found in the middle of an α-helix. Which feature of proline best explains this?
c: Its ring nitrogen forms a tertiary amide with no N–H for helix hydrogen bonding, and the ring restricts backbone rotation
Its side chain is ionized at pH 7 and repels neighboring residues
Its α-carbon is not a stereocenter, so it fits either helix sense
Its amide bond is not planar, because the ring nitrogen cannot share its lone pair with the C=O
h: Look at what is bonded to the nitrogen of proline once it forms a peptide bond.
w: Proline's side chain loops back onto its own α-nitrogen, forming a pyrrolidine ring. When it is acylated in a peptide, that nitrogen becomes a tertiary amide with no N–H, so it cannot donate the i → i + 4 hydrogen bond the helix needs. The ring also locks the N–Cα bond angle (φ), which does not fit the helix. No N–H and a rigid ring; proline acts as a helix breaker and is common in turns.
x: Proline's side chain is a neutral hydrocarbon ring; it is not ionized at any pH.
Proline's α-carbon is a stereocenter (L-proline is S); glycine is the achiral amino acid.
Tertiary amides are still planar and resonance-stabilized; the nitrogen lone pair is delocalized into the C=O just as in other peptide bonds.

q:
Which statements about nucleic acids are correct?
I. 2′-Deoxyribose in DNA lacks the OH group at C2′ that ribose in RNA has.
II. In double-stranded DNA, a purine base pairs with another purine.
III. Thymine and uracil differ only by a methyl group at C5 of the pyrimidine ring.
h: Recall the sugars, the base-pairing rule (one large base with one small base) and the structures of T and U.
w: I is true: DNA uses 2′-deoxyribose, with H instead of OH at C2′. II is false: each Watson–Crick pair joins a purine with a pyrimidine (A–T, G–C), which keeps the helix width constant. III is true: thymine is 5-methyluracil. I and III only.
x: This rejects III, but thymine is exactly uracil with a CH<sub>3</sub> at C5.
This accepts II. Purine–purine pairs would be too wide for the double helix; each pair is purine + pyrimidine.
II is false: base pairs always combine one purine (A or G) with one pyrimidine (T or C).

q: What is the nucleotide shown?
h: Identify three parts: the base (look at C5 and the C4 substituent), the sugar (OH at C2′?) and which carbon carries the phosphate.
w: The base is a pyrimidine with two C=O groups and a CH3 at C5: thymine. The sugar has only a CH2 at C2′, so it is 2′-deoxyribose. The phosphate is on the CH2O (C5′), while C3′ carries a free OH. 2′-Deoxythymidine 5′-monophosphate (dTMP).
x: Uridine has no methyl group on the base, and its ribose has an OH at C2′; this sugar is 2′-deoxy.
Cytosine has an NH<sub>2</sub> at C4 and only one C=O; this base has two C=O groups and a C5 methyl.
The phosphate is attached through the exocyclic CH<sub>2</sub>O, which is C5′. C3′ (on the ring) carries the free OH.

q: In water, sodium stearate (a soap, one C17 tail) forms spherical micelles, while phosphatidylcholine (two C16–C18 tails on one head group) forms bilayer sheets that close into vesicles. What best explains the difference?
c: One tail per head gives a cone shape that packs into a sphere; two tails per head give a cylinder shape that packs into a flat bilayer
The phospholipid head group is nonpolar, so it must be buried inside the sheet
Soap tails are hydrophilic and face the water, while phospholipid tails are hydrophobic
Phospholipids are covalently linked to one another in the bilayer, but soap molecules are not
h: Both molecules hide their hydrocarbon tails from water. Think about how the shape (head size vs tail volume) packs.
w: Both are amphipathic: the polar head faces water and the hydrocarbon tails cluster away from it. A soap has a large head and one thin tail, a cone that packs into a sphere (micelle) with the tails in the core. A phospholipid's two tails take up about as much width as its head, a cylinder, which packs into a flat double layer with the tails inward. The shape set by the number of tails per head decides the aggregate.
x: The phosphocholine head group is ionic (phosphate − and ammonium +) and very polar; it faces the water on both surfaces.
Hydrocarbon tails are hydrophobic in both molecules; in a micelle they form the core, away from water.
Bilayers are held together by noncovalent hydrophobic interactions; no covalent bonds join the lipids.

q: Biodiesel is made by heating a vegetable-oil triacylglycerol with methanol and a catalytic amount of NaOCH<sub>3</sub>. What are the products?
c: Three fatty acid methyl esters (RCO<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>) and glycerol
h: Methoxide attacks an ester carbonyl and the glycerol alkoxide leaves. What kind of reaction swaps one alcohol part of an ester for another?
w: This is base-catalyzed transesterification. Methoxide adds to each ester C=O (tetrahedral intermediate) and the glyceryl alkoxide leaves, giving a methyl ester; the alkoxide takes a proton from methanol, regenerating methoxide. Excess methanol drives all three esters over: three fatty acid methyl esters (biodiesel) and glycerol. The scheme uses a short-chain model triglyceride.
x: Carboxylate salts form when water and a full equivalent of NaOH are used (saponification). Here methoxide is only a catalyst and methanol is the nucleophile.
The acyl groups move to methanol, so the fatty acid parts become methyl esters; glycerol is released as the free triol, not methylated.
Reduction to primary alcohols needs a hydride reagent such as LiAlH<sub>4</sub>. Methoxide only exchanges the alkoxy group.

q: A compound C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>2</sub> shows a strong IR band at 1740 cm<sup>−1</sup> and no band above 3100 cm<sup>−1</sup>. Its <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum is shown. Which structure fits?
h: Five aromatic H means a monosubstituted ring. Where would a CH<sub>2</sub> appear if it were bonded to an ester oxygen and the ring at once?
w: DBE = 5 (ring + C=O); 1740 cm−1 and no O–H means an ester. The 5H multiplet at 7.35 ppm means C6H5–. A 2H singlet at 5.10 ppm is a CH2 bonded to both an ester oxygen and the ring (each shifts it downfield), and the 3H singlet at 2.09 ppm is CH3–C=O. Benzyl acetate, CH3CO2CH2C6H5.
x: Methyl phenylacetate also gives 5H, 2H and 3H singlets, but at about 3.6 (ArCH<sub>2</sub>C=O) and 3.7 ppm (OCH<sub>3</sub>). Nothing would appear at 5.1 ppm.
Ethyl benzoate would show a quartet (≈4.4 ppm, 2H) and a triplet (≈1.4 ppm, 3H) from the ethyl group, with aromatic H near 8.0 ppm.
A para-disubstituted ring gives two 2H doublets, not a 5H multiplet, and this compound has two CH<sub>3</sub> singlets and no CH<sub>2</sub>.

q: A compound C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O has a strong IR band at 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup> and the <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectrum shown. Which structure fits?
h: Five carbons but only three signals: the molecule must have symmetry. Is the 211.8 ppm carbon a ketone or an aldehyde carbon?
w: 1715 cm−1 and a carbon at 211.8 ppm mean a ketone (aldehyde C=O carbons appear near 200 ppm). Only three signals for five carbons requires a mirror plane through the C=O, making the two ethyl groups equivalent: C=O (211.8), CH2 (35.5), CH3 (7.9). Pentan-3-one.
x: Pentan-2-one has no symmetry, so all five carbons are different and give five signals.
3-Methylbutan-2-one has two equivalent CH<sub>3</sub> groups on the CH, but that still leaves four different carbons and four signals.
Pentanal gives five signals, its C=O carbon is near 202 ppm, and its IR would also show aldehyde C–H bands near 2720 and 2820 cm<sup>−1</sup>.

q: (S)-Nicotine (shown) has two nitrogen atoms, a and b. When nicotine is dissolved in a buffer at pH 6, which nitrogen is mostly protonated, and why?
c: a, because its lone pair is in an sp3 orbital, held less tightly than the sp2 lone pair on b
b, because aromatic nitrogens are always more basic than amine nitrogens
a, because its lone pair is part of the aromatic π sextet and is easy to share
b, because its lone pair is delocalized into the ring, which stabilizes the cation
h: Compare a tertiary alkylamine (conjugate acid pK<sub>a</sub> about 8–10) with pyridine (conjugate acid pK<sub>a</sub> about 5). Which lone pair has more s character?
w: Nitrogen a is a tertiary alkylamine (in the pyrrolidine ring): its lone pair is in an sp3 orbital, and its conjugate acid has pKa ≈ 8. Nitrogen b is a pyridine-type nitrogen: its lone pair is in an sp2 orbital (more s character, held closer to the nucleus) and its conjugate acid has pKa ≈ 3. At pH 6, which is below 8 but above 3, a is mostly protonated, because its sp3 lone pair is more available. b stays mostly neutral.
x: Pyridine-type nitrogens are weaker bases than alkylamines (pK<sub>a</sub>H ≈ 5 vs ≈ 10) because the sp<sup>2</sup> lone pair is held closer to the nucleus.
Nitrogen a is in a saturated (pyrrolidine) ring, which is not aromatic; its lone pair is a localized sp3 pair.

The pyridine nitrogen's lone pair lies in the ring plane, perpendicular to the π system, so it is not delocalized; protonating it does not disrupt aromaticity, but the sp<sup>2</sup> pair is still the weaker base.
